title: Time: how we know it is passing, and how clocks and calendars count it

summary.text: A spoonful of salt runs out of a paper cone in about the same time, again and again. That steady running makes the cone a clock. Your child makes this salt timer, tests it, and finds that every clock works by counting something that changes steadily. They put events in order, before and after. They read the family calendar, which in many Indian homes shows two or three dates for one day. They also meet people who picture time as a line, as a wheel, or even running from east to west.
summary.art: A girl of seven watching a thin stream of salt run from a paper cone into a steel tumbler, with a phone stopwatch beside her and a wall calendar behind.

intro.hook: Close your eyes and sit still. Now open them. Did time pass? How do you know?
intro.text: Most children say 'yes', and then find it hard to say how they know. Nobody can see or touch time. We notice it because things change: the fan turns, the light fades, you get hungry. In this unit we look for clues that time has passed. Then we make a clock out of salt and paper, and test whether it keeps steady time.
intro.art: A boy of seven sitting cross-legged with his eyes shut, while behind him the window light changes from afternoon to evening.

outcomes: By the end I can put events in order, saying what came before and what came after.
By the end I can say what every clock needs: something that changes steadily, and a way to count it.
By the end I can make a salt timer, test it several times, and say what I found.
By the end I can put seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years in order, and say that a day is one spin of the Earth and a year is one trip round the Sun.
By the end I can read a wall calendar, and say that India uses more than one calendar.
By the end I can tell two ways people have pictured time: as a line that goes one way, and as a wheel that comes round again.

terms.meaning: Time is how long things take, and the order in which they happen. We cannot see time itself. We notice it when things change.
terms.example: From breakfast to lunch, time passes. The idli plate gets empty and you get hungry again.
terms.art: A plate of idli at breakfast, then the same empty plate, with the sun higher in the window.

terms.meaning: Before means earlier. Something that happens before came first.
terms.example: You brush your teeth before you eat breakfast.
terms.art: A child brushing teeth, with an arrow pointing to the same child eating breakfast.

terms.meaning: After means later. Something that happens after came next.
terms.example: The dosa is cooked after the batter is poured on the tawa.
terms.art: Batter being poured on a hot tawa, and an arrow to a golden folded dosa.

terms.meaning: A change is when something becomes different. Every change takes some time.
terms.example: Ice in a steel plate changes into water.
terms.art: An ice cube on a steel plate, and the same plate later with a small puddle.

terms.meaning: Steady means going on at the same speed, without speeding up or slowing down.
terms.example: A fan on one setting turns at a steady speed.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning, with equal curved lines drawn round it.

terms.meaning: A clock is something that changes steadily, with a way to count the change. The count tells us how much time has passed.
terms.example: A wall clock's hands move steadily round. A salt timer lets salt run out steadily.
terms.art: A round wall clock beside a paper cone dropping salt into a tumbler.

terms.meaning: A timer is a clock that measures one stretch of time, from start to finish.
terms.example: A pressure cooker's whistles and an egg timer are both used as timers in the kitchen.
terms.art: A small sand timer on a kitchen counter next to a pot.

terms.meaning: These are the small units of time. 60 seconds make a minute. 60 minutes make an hour. 24 hours make a day.
terms.example: A blink takes less than a second. Brushing your teeth takes about 2 minutes. A film takes about 2 hours.
terms.art: Three stacked boxes: a tiny one marked 'second', a middle one 'minute', and a big one 'hour'.

terms.meaning: A calendar is a way of counting days, weeks, months and years, and giving each day a name or a number.
terms.example: The wall calendar in the kitchen shows today's date, and the festivals coming up.
terms.art: A wall calendar hanging on a nail in an Indian kitchen, with one date circled.

explanations.context: This card is about a question people have argued over for thousands of years.
explanations.description: Everyone uses time, but nobody agrees exactly what it is. We know time has passed when something changes. Some people say time is just things changing, one after another. Others say time goes on by itself, even if nothing changes. Nobody has found a test to show which is right.
examples: You know the afternoon has passed because the light has changed and you are hungry.
When you wake up, the room looks the same, but the clock and the light at the window tell you night has gone.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, about 2,350 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Time is the counting of change, of what comes before and what comes after. If nothing changed, we could not tell that any time had passed.

perspectives.who: Nagarjuna, a Buddhist teacher in India about 1,800 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Time does not exist on its own, apart from things. Time and the things that change depend on each other.

perspectives.who: Isaac Newton, an English scientist, in 1687
perspectives.explanation: Time flows evenly by itself, whether anything changes or not. Clocks only try to keep up with it.

explanations.art: Three thinkers sitting round a big sand timer: a Greek man in a robe, a Buddhist teacher in South Indian robes, and an English man in a wig.

explanations.definition: Before means earlier in time, and after means later. Putting events in order of before and after is called putting them in sequence.
explanations.context: This card is about putting things in order.
explanations.description: Many things always happen in the same order. A seed sprouts before the plant grows. Milk comes before curd. The order tells us a story about what happened. Often the first thing makes the next thing happen. You cannot get curd without milk first.
examples: Rice and urad dal are soaked, then ground into batter, then left overnight, then cooked into idli.
A mango tree flowers before the mangoes grow.
A caterpillar becomes a butterfly, never the other way round.
explanations.art: Four pictures in a row with arrows: soaking rice, a grinder, a bowl of risen batter, and a plate of idlis.

explanations.definition: A clock is anything that changes at a steady speed, with a way to count the change.
explanations.context: This card explains why your salt timer is a real clock.
explanations.description: In the salt timer, salt runs out at a steady speed. So one spoonful always takes about the same time, and two take about twice as long. Every clock works the same way: something changes steadily, and we count it. Most wristwatches count the shaking of a tiny quartz crystal, 32,768 times every second. The best clocks, atomic clocks, count very fast, steady ticks inside atoms.
examples: A salt or sand timer counts the salt or sand running out.
Long ago in India, a ghati was a small bowl with a hole that floated in water and sank in a set time.
A pendulum clock counts the swings of a weight on a rod.
The Earth spinning once gives us one day.
explanations.art: A row of clocks: a salt timer, a floating bowl, a pendulum clock, a wristwatch and the spinning Earth, each with a small arrow showing what moves.

explanations.concept: Seconds, minutes, hours, days, months and years
explanations.definition: A day is one spin of the Earth. A year is one trip of the Earth round the Sun. A month is about one round of the Moon's shapes. Seconds, minutes, hours and weeks are pieces people chose.
explanations.context: This card is about where our units of time come from.
explanations.description: Some units of time come from the sky. The Earth spins once in a day. The Moon goes from full moon to the next full moon in about 29 and a half days, which is about a month. The Earth goes round the Sun in about 365 and a quarter days, which is a year. People chose the 7-day week, the 24 hours in a day and the 60 minutes in an hour. Long ago in India, a day had 60 nazhigai, and one nazhigai was 24 minutes.
examples: 60 seconds make 1 minute, and 60 minutes make 1 hour.
7 days make a week. Most months have 30 or 31 days.
Every fourth year has one extra day, 29 February, to use up the extra quarter days.
explanations.art: The Earth spinning beside the Sun, the Moon going round it, and a clock face and a calendar page below.

explanations.definition: A calendar is a way of counting days into weeks, months and years. Different calendars count from different starting days.
explanations.context: This card is about the calendars used in India.
explanations.description: Many Indian wall calendars show more than one date for each day. One is the date used across the world, like 2 November. Another may be the Tamil, Malayalam or Bengali date. Many also show the Moon's phase and the Islamic date. The Islamic calendar follows the Moon, so its year is about 11 days shorter. That is why Ramzan comes about 11 days earlier each year.
examples: Onam falls in the Malayalam month of Chingam.
Pohela Boishakh, the Bengali new year, and Puthandu, the Tamil new year, both come in the middle of April.
The names of the weekdays come from the Sun, the Moon and five planets: Ravivar or Nyayiru is the Sun's day, Somavar or Thingal is the Moon's day.
explanations.art: A colourful Indian wall calendar page with big numbers, small Tamil numbers, Moon shapes and festival names.

explanations.context: This card is about different ways people picture time.
explanations.description: People picture time in different ways. Some see a line, going one way, from the past to the future. Others see a wheel, where things come round again. Days, weeks, seasons and festivals do come round. But a broken glass never mends itself, and you never grow younger.
examples: Jain teachings picture time as a great wheel, the kalachakra, with one half turning towards better ages and one half towards worse ages.
Hindu teachings tell of four ages, the yugas, that come round again and again.
Many people who read English, Hindi or Tamil lay out the past on the left. Many who read Urdu or Arabic lay it out on the right.

perspectives.who: People who picture time as a line
perspectives.explanation: Time goes one way only. Each day happens once and never again. You grow older, never younger.

perspectives.who: People who picture time as a wheel
perspectives.explanation: Time turns round and round. Morning, the rains and Pongal all come back. The world goes through the same ages again and again.
Small things repeat, like days and years. But the whole universe has a history that goes one way. It began about 13.8 billion years ago and has been changing ever since.

explanations.art: On one side a long road with milestones going into the distance, and on the other a big turning wheel with seasons painted on its spokes.

explanations.context: This card is about the clocks inside living beings.
explanations.description: You are not the only one who keeps time. Bean plants lift their leaves before the morning comes. Crows fly home to their trees at dusk. Even tiny bacteria keep a daily clock. Living beings sense the day, remember its rhythm and get ready for what comes next. Some scientists call these body clocks and describe how they work as chemistry.
examples: You feel sleepy at about the same time each night.
A rooster starts crowing just before dawn.
Jasmine buds open in the evening.
explanations.art: Bean plants lifting their leaves at dawn beside a window, with a crow on the ledge and a sleeping child inside.

agreed.text: A day is the time the Earth takes to spin once. A year is the time the Earth takes to go once round the Sun, about 365 and a quarter days.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers have measured the Earth's spin and its path round the Sun for thousands of years, from India, China, Babylon, Greece and the Maya lands, and the numbers agree.

agreed.text: Every clock works by counting something that changes steadily.
agreed.evidence: Sand timers, water clocks, pendulum clocks, quartz watches and atomic clocks all do this. A clock is only as good as its steady change.

agreed.text: Atomic clocks are the most exact clocks people have made. Since 1967, one second has been measured with them.
agreed.evidence: Scientists everywhere agreed to define one second as 9,192,631,770 ticks inside a caesium atom. Good atomic clocks lose less than one second in millions of years.

agreed.text: Indian Standard Time is kept by atomic clocks at the CSIR-National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi.
agreed.evidence: The laboratory keeps India's official time and shares it so that phones, trains and offices agree. Indian Standard Time is 5 and a half hours ahead of the world's standard time.

challenging.claim: Time goes at exactly the same speed everywhere.
challenging.for: Clocks in Chennai and Kolkata agree, and a day feels the same length everywhere.
challenging.against: Albert Einstein worked out that clocks higher up, or moving very fast, tick a tiny bit differently. Very exact atomic clocks have shown this.
challenging.context: This card is about whether time is the same for everyone. You will learn more about it in a later unit.

challenging.claim: Time is a wheel, and everything comes round again.
challenging.who: Jain and Hindu teachings, and some old Greek thinkers
challenging.for: Days, months, seasons and festivals really do come round again and again.
challenging.against: Some changes never come back. A broken egg stays broken, and a person grows older, never younger.
challenging.context: This card is about time as a wheel.

challenging.claim: Time is only in our minds.
challenging.who: Some philosophers, such as Immanuel Kant of Germany
challenging.for: Time feels fast when we play and slow when we wait, though the clock moves the same.
challenging.against: Clocks, seasons and growing plants keep time even when nobody is watching them.
challenging.context: This card is about whether time is out in the world or inside us.

big_questions.q: If everything in the world stopped changing, even your heartbeat, would time still pass?
big_questions.hint: Think about how you knew that time passed in the salt timer. What would you have to watch if nothing changed?

big_questions.q: Your salt timer and the Earth both count time. Is one of them the real time?
big_questions.hint: Each one counts a steady change. Which change is steadier, and who decides which one to trust?

big_questions.q: Why do we remember yesterday but not tomorrow?
big_questions.hint: Think about which way changes go. Do you ever see batter turn back into rice?
Scientists say the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago. Ask what came before, and whether 'before' makes sense then.

big_questions.q: A minute of waiting feels long, and a minute of play feels short. Which one is the true minute?
big_questions.hint: The clock counts one steady change. Your feeling counts something else. What does it count?

story.title: The Salt Clock in the Power Cut
story.note: Kavya, Arjun, Amma and Paati are made up. Paati means grandmother in Tamil, and Amma means mother. The facts in the story are true: Aippasi is a Tamil month in October and November, when the northeast monsoon brings heavy rain to Tamil Nadu. Salt runs from a cone at a steady speed, and many Tamil wall calendars show the Tamil date under the date used across the world.
text: Kavya was seven. She lived in a flat on the third floor in Madurai, with her mother Amma, her grandmother Paati and her little brother Arjun. Arjun was five.

It was the month of Aippasi, when the big rains come to Madurai. One evening the rain poured down, and the power went off. The fan stopped. The fridge went quiet. The flat was dark except for one torch.
Kavya held the torch to make shadow animals on the wall. Arjun wanted it too. 'My turn!' he said. 'You had it for ages!'
'I only had it for a little bit,' said Kavya.

Paati looked up from her chair. 'How long is a little bit? And how long is ages?' she asked. Nobody knew. The phones were nearly out of charge, and the wall clock had stopped. Its battery had run out that morning.
'Then we will make a clock,' said Paati. Kavya laughed. 'You can't make a clock, Paati. You buy it from a shop.'

Paati took a page from an old notebook. She rolled it into a cone and pinned it with a hairpin. With the kitchen scissors she snipped off the tip, leaving a small hole. She set the cone in the mouth of a steel tumbler.

'Bring the salt dabba,' said Paati. Kavya brought it. Paati put one finger under the hole and filled the cone with one big spoon of salt. 'Now, Kavya, hold the torch. Arjun, you watch the salt. When the last salt falls, it is your turn.' She took her finger away.

A thin white stream ran down into the tumbler. Arjun watched it like a hawk. Kavya made a rabbit, a dog and a flying crow on the wall. Then the last salt fell. 'Your turn!' Kavya said, and handed over the torch.
Paati poured the salt back into the cone. Now Kavya watched the stream while Arjun made shadows. Turn by turn, they took the torch. Nobody said 'ages' any more.
Then Arjun had an idea. When it was Kavya's turn, he put in only half a spoon of salt. The stream ran out very quickly. 'Your turn is over!' he said.
'That's not fair!' said Kavya. 'You put in less salt.'

'Kavya is right,' said Paati. 'The salt runs out at a steady speed. So the same spoon of salt takes the same time, every time. Half the salt gives half the time. That is the only thing that makes this cone a clock.'
Kavya thought about this. 'So the clock is just salt running,' she said slowly. 'And the wall clock is just its hands going round. And the time, where is the time?'

Paati smiled. 'People have asked that for thousands of years,' she said. 'We never see time itself. We only see things change: salt falling, hands going round, the rain stopping. We count the steady changes, and we call that counting time.'
Just then the fan whirred and the lights came on. The fridge hummed. Amma came out of the kitchen and looked at the phone. 'The power was off for forty minutes,' she said.
Kavya looked at the tumbler. It was full of salt that had run through again and again. 'We counted those forty minutes too,' she said, 'in spoons of salt.'

Before bed, Kavya looked at the wall calendar. Under the big number for the day was a small Tamil date for Aippasi, and a little drawing of the Moon. 'Paati, why does one day have two dates?' she asked.
'Because people have more than one way of counting days,' said Paati. 'The Sun counts one way and the Moon another. But the day is the same day.'
The next evening, Kavya showed Arjun how to make the cone himself. 'Always one full spoon,' she told him. 'Then it is fair.' Arjun filled it carefully, right to the brim of the spoon.
story.epiphany: Kavya sees that the salt cone is a clock only because the salt runs out at a steady speed. A clock does not hold time inside it. People find time by counting a steady change, whether it is salt, wheels or days.
ask: Why did Kavya and Arjun quarrel over the torch?
How did Paati make a clock from things in the kitchen?
Why was Arjun's half-spoon trick not fair?
Kavya asked, 'Where is the time?' What did Paati say?

games.title: Before or After? a two-sided card game
games.context: This is a card game about putting things in order. Each card names two things. Players say which one comes first, then turn the card over to check.

items.f: Milk or curd: which comes first?
items.b: Milk. Curd is made by leaving warm milk with a spoon of old curd.

items.f: Dosa or batter: which comes first?
items.b: Batter. It is poured on a hot tawa to make the dosa.

items.f: Seed or plant: which comes first?
items.b: Seed. A seed sprouts and grows into a plant.

items.f: Egg or chick: which comes first, for this one chick?
items.b: Egg. The chick grows inside the egg, then hatches.

items.f: Caterpillar or butterfly: which comes first?
items.b: Caterpillar. The caterpillar makes a hard case around herself and comes out as a butterfly.

items.f: Mango flower or mango: which comes first?
items.b: Flower. Bees and other insects visit the flower, then the mango grows.

items.f: Rain or puddle: which comes first?
items.b: Rain. The rain falls and the water collects in a puddle.

items.f: An ice cube melts on a plate. Ice or water: which comes first?
items.b: Ice. The ice melted into water.

items.f: Thunder or lightning: which do you notice first?
items.b: Lightning. The light reaches you before the sound.

items.f: Baby teeth or grown-up teeth: which come first?
items.b: Baby teeth. They fall out and grown-up teeth grow in.

items.f: Cotton or shirt: which comes first?
items.b: Cotton. Cotton is spun into thread and woven into cloth.

items.f: Full moon or new moon: which comes first?
items.b: Both. Each one comes after the other, again and again, about every two weeks.

rules: Cut out the 12 cards. Fold or stick each one so the question is on the front and the answer is on the back.
Put the cards in a pile, question side up.
Take turns. Read the top card aloud and say which comes first, and why.
Turn the card over. If your answer matches the back, keep the card.
If it does not match, put the card to one side. Read the back aloud together so everyone learns it.
The moon card is special. Saying 'both', or saying one of them and giving the reason 'they take turns', wins the card.
When the pile is gone, the player with the most cards wins. With two players, each count your cards. If you have the same number, you both win.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Read two cards aloud with your child. 3. Pile the rest question side up.
flow.say: Each card shows two things. Your job is to say which one comes first, and why.
flow.kid: Each card has two things. Which one comes first?

flow.do: Take turns reading and answering. Ask for the reason every time.
flow.say: Milk or curd? Which comes first? How do you know?
flow.kid: Say which comes first. Then say why.

ask.q: How do you know which comes first?
good: Curd is made from milk.
You need the seed to get the plant.
The ice melted, so the ice was there before the water.

flow.parent: The reason matters more than the answer. A strong reason says how the first thing makes the second, like 'curd is made from milk'.

flow.do: Talk about the moon card.
flow.say: The moon card said both. Why is that?
flow.kid: Why can the full moon and the new moon both come first?

good: They take turns.
They come round again and again, like a wheel.

flow.parent: This card shows things that come round in a cycle. In a cycle, nothing is first for good. This links to the 'line or wheel' idea.

flow.do: Count the cards and find the winner.
flow.say: Which card was the hardest? Why?
flow.kid: Which card was the hardest for you?
flow.think: Can you think of two things where the order can go either way?

experiments.title: The Salt Timer: does each spoonful take the same time?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child makes a timer from a paper cone and salt. They time one spoonful three times, then two spoonfuls twice. They find out whether the timer is steady enough to be a clock.
experiments.question: Does one spoon of salt take the same time to run out of a paper cone every time? Do two spoons take twice as long?
experiments.predict: Will one spoon of salt take the same time every try? Will two spoons take twice as long, or less, or more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same cone, the same salt and the same spoon every time. Each spoon is filled level, not heaped. We start and stop the stopwatch the same way every time. Only one thing changes: one spoon or two. We try each one more than once, because one try can be a lucky or unlucky one.

materials.item: a sheet of notebook paper or newspaper
sticky tape or a hairpin
scissors
a steel tumbler or a glass
dry table salt, about 4 big spoons (dry rava or sugar also works)
a big spoon (a tablespoon)
a phone with a stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a bowl to pour the salt back into

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a row of boxes for each try, one box for every 5 seconds, and colour them in.

setup.caption: 2. Snip off the tip to make a small hole.

setup.caption: 3. Finger under the hole. Pour in one level spoon of salt.

flow.do: 1. Roll the paper into a cone and tape it. 2. Snip the tip off so the hole is about 3 millimetres wide, smaller than a peppercorn. 3. Sit the cone in the mouth of the tumbler.
flow.say: We are making a timer out of paper and salt. The hole must be small, so the salt runs out slowly.
flow.kid: Roll the paper into a cone. A grown-up snips a tiny hole at the tip.
flow.parent: If the salt runs out in under 10 seconds, the hole is too big. Make a new cone and snip less. If the salt sticks, a grown-up can dry it on a warm tawa for a minute (let it cool), or use dry rava. In the monsoon, salt often clumps, so keep it in a closed dabba.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before the first try. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: How many seconds will one spoon of salt take to run out? Will it be the same every time? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: how many seconds for one spoon? Same every time? Why?

good: Yes, because it is the same salt and the same hole.
No, because the salt might get stuck.
It will slow down at the end, like water does.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. Many children think the salt will slow down at the end. Let the test answer it.

flow.do: 1. Hold a finger under the hole. 2. Pour in one level spoon of salt. 3. Say 'go', take the finger away, and start the stopwatch. 4. Stop it when the last salt falls.
flow.say: Watch the stream. Tell me the moment it stops.
flow.kid: Watch the salt. Shout 'stop' when the last salt falls.
flow.parent: Your child watches the stream and you work the stopwatch, or the other way round. Write the seconds in the table. Pour the salt from the tumbler back into the bowl.

flow.do: Do the same with one spoon two more times. Write each time.
flow.say: Let's try one spoon again. Was it the same as last time?
flow.kid: Do it two more times. Are the times close?
flow.parent: The times usually come within a second or two of each other. If one try is very different, ask what went wrong. Perhaps the spoon was heaped, or salt stuck to the side.

flow.do: Now pour in two level spoons and time it. Do this twice.
flow.say: Two spoons now. Before we start, how long do you think it will take? Why?
flow.kid: Now try two spoons. Guess first. Then time it twice.
flow.parent: Two spoons usually take about twice as long as one. It may be a few seconds more or less.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: What did you find out? Which numbers show it? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: What did you find? Which numbers show it?

good: One spoon took about the same time each try.
Two spoons took about twice as long as one.
The salt did not slow down at the end.

check.q: One spoon took 20 seconds. About how long will two spoons take?
check.why: The salt runs at a steady speed. So twice the salt takes about twice the time: 20 and 20 make 40.

flow.do: Tell your child why the timer works.
flow.say: The salt ran out at a steady speed. That is why your cone is a real clock. Every clock in the world counts some steady change like this.
flow.kid: Your salt ran at a steady speed. That makes it a clock.
flow.think: What other steady changes could you use as a clock?
flow.parent: Sand and salt grains run out at nearly the same speed, however much is left above them. Water is different: it runs out more slowly as the bottle empties. That is why sand timers were so useful.

experiments.title: Which Way Does Time Go? The banana card test with your family
experiments.context: In this experiment your child asks family members to lay four picture cards in order, from first to last. They record which way each person lays out time: left to right, right to left, or another way.
experiments.question: When people lay out pictures in order of time, which way do they go?
experiments.predict: Will everyone in the family lay the cards from left to right? Will anyone go another way? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Everyone gets the same four cards, mixed up the same way. We say the same words to everyone: 'Put these in order, from first to last.' We never say left or right. Each person does it alone, without watching the others.
results_table: Which way they laid the cards

materials.item: 4 small squares of paper, about the size of a playing card
a pencil or crayons
a table or a clear patch of floor
3 or more people to ask: family, neighbours or friends, at home or on a video call

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw an arrow for each person showing the way their cards went.

setup.art: Four small cards: a whole banana, a banana half peeled, a banana half eaten, and only the peel.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four banana cards.

setup.art: A grandmother laying four banana cards in a row on a table while a girl watches with a notebook.
setup.caption: 2. Ask each person to put the cards in order.

setup.art: A notebook page with arrows: three pointing right and one pointing left.
setup.caption: 3. Draw an arrow for the way each person went.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws four cards: a whole banana, a banana half peeled, a banana half eaten, and only the peel. 2. Mix them up.
flow.say: We are going to find out which way people lay out time. First, draw the four banana cards.
flow.kid: Draw four banana cards: whole, half peeled, half eaten, only the peel.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Will everyone put the cards from left to right? Will anyone go another way? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess: which way will each person go? Why?

good: Left to right, because that is how we read.
Someone who reads Urdu may go another way.
A young child who cannot read yet may put them in a pile.

flow.do: 1. Give each person the mixed cards. 2. Say only: 'Put these in order, from first to last.' 3. Watch where they put the first card and the last card. 4. Ask which languages they read.
flow.say: Please put these in order, from first to last.
flow.kid: Say: put these in order, from first to last. Watch which way they go.
flow.parent: Never say left or right. On a video call, ask the person to hold their row up to the camera. Note that the picture on a phone camera may be flipped, so ask them to point to the first card.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: Which way did most people go? Did anyone go a different way? What might explain it?
flow.kid: Which way did most people go? Did anyone go another way?

good: Everyone reads Tamil and English from left to right.
One person reads Urdu, which goes from right to left.
A child who cannot read yet made a pile.

flow.parent: In many Indian homes everyone goes left to right, because Tamil, Hindi, English and most Indian scripts are written left to right. That is a real result. People who read Urdu or Arabic, written right to left, more often lay out time from right to left.

flow.do: Tell your child what scientists have found.
flow.say: Scientists have found that people often lay out time the way they read. In one Aboriginal community in Australia, people lay out time from east to west.
flow.kid: People often lay out time the way they read.
flow.think: If you faced the other way, would your cards still go the same way?

activities.title: Time Clues: what shows that time has passed?
activities.context: This short hunt starts the unit. Your child looks around the flat for clues that time has passed, and thinks about how they know.

materials.item: an ice cube on a steel plate, put out at the start
a photo of your child as a baby, on a phone or in an album

setup.art: A girl kneeling by a steel plate with a half-melted ice cube, and a balcony with drying clothes behind her.
setup.caption: 1. Look for things that have changed.

setup.art: A girl holding a phone with a baby photo next to her own smiling face.
setup.caption: 2. Compare a baby photo with you now.

flow.do: Put an ice cube on a steel plate where your child can see it.
flow.say: We will come back to this ice cube in a few minutes. Look at it carefully now.
flow.kid: Look at the ice cube. We will come back to it.

flow.do: Walk round the flat together. Find five clues that time has passed today.
flow.say: Can you find five things that show time has passed since this morning? How do you know?
flow.kid: Find five things that show time has passed today.

good: The clothes on the line are dry now.
The milk in the vessel has set into curd.
The light at the window has moved.
My plate is empty and I am hungry again.

flow.parent: Any change counts: drying clothes, risen dosa batter, a wilting flower, a new newspaper, the light. Point out that every clue is a change.

flow.do: Look at the ice cube again. Then look at the baby photo together.
flow.say: What happened to the ice cube? And look at you as a baby. What has changed?
flow.kid: Look at the ice cube now. Look at your baby photo. What changed?
flow.parent: A small ice cube on a steel plate in a warm flat is mostly melted in about 8 to 10 minutes. If it is still a big lump, say it has changed a little, and look again later.

flow.do: Ask the big question, and let your child think.
flow.say: Every clue was a change. If nothing at all had changed, how would you know time had passed?
flow.kid: If nothing changed, would you know time had passed?

good: I would not know.
I would still feel hungry.
My heart would still beat.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer. Many grown-ups find this hard too. Tell your child that people have argued about it for thousands of years.

activities.title: First, Next, Then, Last: draw your morning in four boxes
activities.context: In this activity your child draws four things they did this morning, cuts them apart, mixes them up, and puts them back in order.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded into four boxes
crayons
scissors

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into four boxes, with a child drawing waking up in the first box.
setup.caption: 1. Draw four things from your morning.

setup.art: Four cut-out drawings mixed up on the floor, and a hand moving one into place.
setup.caption: 2. Mix them up and put them back in order.

flow.do: Your child draws four things from this morning, one in each box.
flow.say: Draw four things you did this morning, in the order you did them.
flow.kid: Draw four things you did this morning, in order.

flow.do: 1. Cut the boxes apart. 2. Mix them up. 3. Your child puts them back in order and says each one aloud.
flow.say: Put them back in order. Say first, next, then and last.
flow.kid: Put them back in order. Say first, next, then, last.

flow.do: Ask which pairs can swap and which cannot.
flow.say: Could you swap any two pictures and still have a true morning? Which two can never swap?
flow.kid: Which two pictures can swap? Which two never can?

good: Waking up must come before everything else.
Eating must come before washing my plate.
Brushing and bathing could swap.

flow.parent: Some orders are fixed, because one thing causes or needs the other. Some are only habits. Both are kinds of before and after.

activities.title: How Many Dates Does Today Have? The wall calendar hunt
activities.context: In this activity your child reads the family's wall calendar, or a calendar on the phone, and finds out how many ways today is named.

materials.item: a wall calendar, a diary or a calendar on a phone
a pencil and paper

setup.art: A girl standing on tiptoe pointing at today's date on a colourful Indian wall calendar.
setup.caption: 1. Find today on the calendar.

setup.art: A close-up of one calendar box with a big number, a small Tamil date, and a little Moon shape.
setup.caption: 2. Count every date and sign for today.

flow.do: Find today's date on the calendar together.
flow.say: Can you find today on the calendar? What day of the week is it? What is the month?
flow.kid: Find today on the calendar. What day is it?

flow.do: Look closely at today's box. Count every date or sign in it.
flow.say: Look at today's box. How many different dates or signs can you find?
flow.kid: Count every date and sign in today's box.
flow.parent: Many Indian calendars show the date used across the world, a regional date such as Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, Kannada, Bengali or Marathi, the Moon's phase, and sometimes the Islamic date. If your calendar has only one date, look at a regional calendar on the phone together.

flow.do: Count the days in this month, and find one festival or birthday.
flow.say: How many days are in this month? How many days until the next festival or birthday?
flow.kid: Count the days in this month. Find the next festival.

flow.do: Ask why one day can have more than one date.
flow.say: Why do you think one day has more than one date?
flow.kid: Why does one day have more than one date?

good: People count days in different ways.
Some calendars follow the Moon and some follow the Sun.

activities.title: Line or Wheel? Draw your week two ways
activities.context: In this activity your child draws the days of the week as a straight line and as a wheel, and talks about which picture fits time better.

materials.item: two sheets of paper
crayons
a steel plate or a lid to draw round

setup.art: A long strip of paper with seven boxes for the days of the week, each with a small drawing.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your week as a line.

setup.art: A circle drawn round a steel plate, cut into seven slices like a wheel, one for each day.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your week as a wheel.

flow.do: Your child draws seven boxes in a row and writes one day in each, with something they do on that day.
flow.say: Let's draw the week as a line. Monday first. What do you do on each day?
flow.kid: Draw seven boxes in a row. One box for each day.

flow.do: Draw round a plate to make a circle. Divide it into seven slices, like a wheel. Fill in the days again.
flow.say: Now draw the same week as a wheel. What comes after Sunday on the wheel?
flow.kid: Now draw the week as a wheel. What comes after Sunday?

flow.do: Talk about which picture fits better.
flow.say: Which picture is true? The days do come round again. But you will never have last Monday again. What do you think?
flow.kid: Which picture fits time better? Why?

good: The wheel, because Monday comes back every week.
The line, because last Monday is gone for good.
Both, because the days come back but I keep growing.

flow.parent: Both pictures are true of something. Let your child choose one and give a reason.

activities.title: The Clock Hunt: do all the clocks at home agree?
activities.context: In this activity your child finds every clock in the flat and checks whether they all show the same time.

materials.item: every clock in the flat: wall clock, phone, microwave, television box, wristwatch
a pencil and paper

setup.art: A boy with a notebook looking at the clock on a microwave, with a wall clock and a phone nearby.
setup.caption: 1. Find every clock in the flat.

setup.art: A notebook page listing clocks and their times, two of them a minute or two different.
setup.caption: 2. Write down the time on each one, quickly.

flow.do: Walk round the flat together and write down the time each clock shows. Move quickly, so little time passes between clocks.
flow.say: Let's find every clock at home. Write down the time each one shows. Be quick!
flow.kid: Find every clock. Write down the time each one shows.

flow.do: Compare the times.
flow.say: Do all the clocks agree? Which ones are different? By how much?
flow.kid: Do they all agree? Which ones are different?
flow.parent: Clocks often differ by a minute or more. A phone sets itself from the mobile network, which gets its time from very exact clocks. A microwave clock is set by hand and drifts a little.

flow.do: Ask which clock to trust.
flow.say: If the clocks disagree, which one would you trust? Why?
flow.kid: Which clock would you trust? Why?

good: The phone, because it sets itself.
I would check them against each other.

flow.parent: India's official time is kept by atomic clocks at the National Physical Laboratory in New Delhi. Phones get their time from that kind of clock, through the network.

projects.title: A Paper-Chain Countdown to a day you are waiting for
projects.context: In this project your child makes a paper chain with one loop for each day until a festival, a birthday or a visit. Each morning they tear off one loop, and watch the wait get shorter.

materials.item: strips of old newspaper or coloured paper, about two fingers wide
glue or sticky tape
a calendar

schedule.what: Count the days on the calendar. Make one loop for each day and join them into a chain.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off one loop. Count the loops left.
Tear off the last loop. The day has come. Talk about how the wait felt.

projects.record: Write the number of loops left each morning. At the end, draw the chain getting shorter.

setup.art: A girl gluing paper strips into loops to make a colourful chain, with a calendar open beside her.
setup.caption: 1. Make one loop for each day you must wait.

setup.art: A paper chain hanging from a door handle, with one loop torn off and lying on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Tear off one loop each morning.

flow.do: Choose a day your child is waiting for, 7 days away. Count the days to it on the calendar.
flow.say: Which day are you waiting for? Let's count how many days away it is.
flow.kid: Choose a day you are waiting for. Count the days to it.

flow.do: Make one paper loop for each day, joining each loop through the last one.
flow.say: Make one loop for each day. How long will the chain be?
flow.kid: Make one loop for each day. Join them into a chain.

flow.do: Each morning, from the day after you make the chain, your child tears off one loop and counts the loops left.
flow.say: Tear off one loop. How many days are left now?
flow.kid: Tear off one loop. Count how many are left.
flow.wait: Do this every morning until the day comes. The last loop is torn off on that day.

flow.do: On the day itself, talk about the chain.
flow.say: Did the wait feel the same every day? Did some days feel longer?
flow.kid: Did some days feel longer than others?

ask.q: Did the days feel the same?
good: The last days felt slow because I was excited.
The calendar days were the same length, but they felt different.

flow.parent: Each day lasts the same 24 hours by the clock. How long it feels depends on what we are doing and feeling. Scientists still study why.

flow.do: Ask what the chain measured.
flow.say: What did the chain count? Was it time, or was it mornings?
flow.kid: What did your chain count?
flow.think: Could you make a chain for a whole year? How many loops would it need?

challenges.title: A Fair-Turn Timer: make a salt timer that lasts one minute
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Two children want fair turns with one toy. Can you make a salt timer that runs for one minute, so every turn is the same length?
challenges.problem: Make a salt timer that runs out in one minute, give or take 5 seconds.
constraints: Use only paper, tape, salt, a spoon and a tumbler.
The timer must work three times in a row.
Use the phone stopwatch only to check your timer while you make it.
materials: a paper cone with a small hole
general: Time one spoon of salt. Then work out how many spoons make about 60 seconds.
Add salt a little at a time until it runs for one minute.
Mark a line on the cone to show how full to fill it every time.
creative: Make the hole smaller with a piece of tape, so the salt runs more slowly.
Make two cones, one for 30 seconds and one for a minute.
Colour the salt with a little turmeric so the stream is easy to see.
challenges.your_turn: Now make your own one-minute timer. Mark the fill line on the cone. Use it to share a toy or a game with someone at home, and see if the turns feel fair.

setup.art: A girl pouring salt into a paper cone that has a pencil line drawn inside, near the top.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the cone to the line.

setup.art: Two children sharing a spinning top, with a salt timer running on the table between them.
setup.caption: 2. Use your timer for fair turns.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Ask how to start.
flow.say: We need a timer that runs for one minute. One minute is 60 seconds. How could we start?
flow.kid: We need a one-minute timer. How could we start?

good: Time one spoon first.
Keep adding salt until it is one minute.

flow.do: Your child tries their plan, checking each try with the stopwatch.
flow.say: Try it. How many seconds did it take? Do we need more salt or less?
flow.kid: Try it. Is it more or less than 60 seconds?
flow.parent: If one spoon took 20 seconds, three spoons should take about 60. Let your child work this out by counting on in 20s.

flow.do: When it runs for about a minute, mark the fill line and test it three more times.
flow.say: Draw a line where the salt comes up to. Now test it three times.
flow.kid: Draw a fill line. Test it three times.

flow.do: Ask what makes it fair.
flow.say: Why is your timer fair for both children?
flow.kid: Why is your timer fair?

good: It is the same amount of salt every time.
The salt runs at a steady speed, so every turn is the same.

quiz.p: Which happens first when making dosa?
opts: The dosa is eaten
The batter is poured on the tawa
The rice and dal are soaked
quiz.why: Rice and dal are soaked first, then ground into batter, then poured on the tawa, and then the dosa is eaten.

opts: Something that changes at a steady speed
A battery
Numbers on a round face
quiz.why: A salt timer has no battery and no numbers, but it is still a clock. Every clock needs a steady change, and a way to count it.

quiz.p: In the salt-timer test, why did we fill the spoon level every time, not heaped?
opts: So each spoon held the same amount of salt
So the salt would taste better
So the cone would not tear
quiz.why: A heaped spoon holds more salt, and more salt takes longer. A level spoon keeps the test fair.

quiz.p: Which of these is the longest?
opts: An hour
A day
A week
quiz.why: A week is 7 days. A day is 24 hours. So a week is the longest.

quiz.p: Why is a day as long as it is?
opts: The Earth spins once in a day
The Sun stops shining at night
Clocks decide it
quiz.why: One day is one spin of the Earth. The Sun keeps shining all the time. Clocks only count the day into hours.

quiz.p: About how many days are in a month?
opts: About 7
About 30
About 365
quiz.why: Most months have 30 or 31 days. A week has 7 days, and a year has 365.

quiz.p: Many Indian wall calendars show two or three dates for one day. Why?
opts: People in India use more than one calendar
The printer made a mistake
To fill up the empty space
quiz.why: India uses the calendar shared across the world, regional calendars such as the Tamil or Bengali one, and the Islamic calendar. Each counts the same day in its own way.

quiz.p: In the banana card test, which way do most people who read Tamil, Hindi or English lay out time?
opts: From left to right
From right to left
From bottom to top
quiz.why: People often lay out time the way they read. Tamil, Hindi and English are written from left to right.

quiz.p: Jain teachings picture time as which of these?
opts: A wheel that keeps turning
A ladder with a top step
A box with a lid
quiz.why: Jain teachings picture time as a great wheel, the kalachakra, that keeps turning through better and worse ages.

quiz.p: A wall clock is steady but shows 5 minutes late. It can still be a good clock once it is set right.
quiz.why: True. A steady clock only needs to be set right once. A clock that speeds up and slows down is the real problem.

worksheets.title: Before and after, and the salt timer

items.p: Put these in order, from first to last.
items: rice and urad dal are soaked
the soaked rice and dal are ground
a: rice and urad dal are soaked
the soaked rice and dal are ground
items.why: Each step needs the one before it. You cannot grind dal that has not been soaked, or steam batter that has not been made.

items.p: Draw your salt timer. Draw the cone, the hole, the salt stream and the tumbler.
items.a: A cone with a small hole at the bottom, a thin line of salt falling, and a tumbler below.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the small hole, because the hole decides how fast the salt runs.
items.art: An empty box with a dotted outline of a tumbler.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: did one spoon of salt take the same time every try? Which numbers show it?
items.a: For example: 'Almost. It took 18, 19 and 18 seconds. The times were very close.'
items.why: A strong answer gives the real numbers from the table as evidence.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to about how long it takes.
pairs: A baby growing inside the mother
items.why: These go from the shortest to the longest. A blink is over in a flash, and a baby takes most of a year to grow.

items.p: A clock has time stored inside it.
items.why: False. A clock holds something that changes steadily, like salt running or a crystal shaking. We count the change and call it time.

items.p: The salt ran out at a ________ speed, so each spoonful took about the same time.
items.why: Steady means the same speed all the way through. That is what makes the salt cone a clock.

items.p: Meera, a girl of 7 in Kochi, and her friend Farhana, a girl of 8 in Hyderabad, are talking about clocks.

views.says: A salt timer is not a real clock. A real clock has numbers and hands.
A salt timer is a real clock, because the salt runs out in the same time every time.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Farhana, because my salt took 18 seconds every time.' Then it is fair to Meera: a wall clock is easier to read, and it can count a whole day.
items.why: Both girls see something true. A clock needs a steady change, which the salt has. Numbers and hands make a clock easier to read, but they are not what makes it a clock.

items.p: Three of these can help you tell how much time has passed. Which one cannot?
opts: A salt timer
The wall calendar
The colour of your shirt
The Sun moving across the sky
items.why: Your shirt stays the same colour all day. The salt, the calendar and the Sun all change steadily, so we can count them.

items.p: Sort each pair: which comes first, and which comes later?
items.why: In each pair, the first thing becomes the second. A bud opens into a flower, flour is made into a roti, and wet clothes dry on the line.

items.p: A salt timer ran out too fast, in only 3 seconds. What should the maker change?
opts: Make the hole smaller
Make the hole bigger
Use a bigger tumbler
items.why: A smaller hole lets less salt through each second. So the same salt takes longer to run out.

items.p: Here is one box from a Tamil wall calendar. Label the date used across the world, the Tamil date, and the Moon sign.
items.a: The big number is the date used across the world. The small number with the Tamil month is the Tamil date. The little circle or crescent is the Moon sign.
items.why: A strong answer finds all three, and knows they all name the same day.
items.art: One calendar box with a big '2', a small Tamil date with the month Aippasi, and a small half-Moon drawing.

items.p: What is one year?
opts: The time the Earth takes to go once round the Sun
The time the Moon takes to go from full to new
The time the Earth takes to spin once
items.why: A year is one trip of the Earth round the Sun, about 365 and a quarter days. Every birthday comes round once a year because of this.

items.p: Every calendar used in India starts the new year on 1 January.
items.why: False. The Tamil and Bengali new years come in the middle of April. The Islamic new year moves round the year, because it follows the Moon.

items.p: There are ____ days in a week, and ____ hours in a day.
items.why: A week is 7 days. A day, one spin of the Earth, is counted as 24 hours.

items.p: Name two things that come round again, like Monday. Name two things that never come back.
items.a: For example: 'Monday and the rains come round again. Yesterday and my baby days never come back.'
items.why: A strong answer separates things that repeat, like days and seasons, from changes that cannot be undone.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl of 8 in Mysuru, and Ketki, a girl of 8 in Pune, are arguing about time.

views.says: Time is a line. Yesterday is gone and never comes back.
Time is a wheel. Monday comes back every week, and the rains come back every year.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Ketki, because Pongal comes every year.' Then it is fair to Lakshmi: I will never be 5 again.
items.why: Both views are old and both see something true. Days and seasons come round, but some changes never go back.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest to the longest.
items.why: 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes an hour, 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, about 30 days a month, and 12 months a year.

items.p: Why does Ramzan come about 11 days earlier each year?
opts: The Islamic calendar follows the Moon, and its year is about 11 days shorter
People choose a new date each year
The Sun moves faster in some years
items.why: Twelve rounds of the Moon take about 354 days. The Sun's year is about 365 days. So the Moon's year ends about 11 days sooner, and Ramzan moves earlier.

items.p: A film is 2 hours long. How many minutes is that?
items.why: One hour is 60 minutes. 60 and 60 make 120.

items.p: Draw a line from each unit of time to where it comes from.
pairs: The Earth going once round the Sun
The Moon going through all its shapes
items.why: Days, months and years come from the sky. The hour is a piece that people chose.

worksheets.title: How do we know time is passing?

items.p: Rekha, a woman who teaches science in Chennai, and Mou, a girl of 9 in Kolkata, disagree.

views.says: Time goes on by itself, even if nothing changes. Clocks only try to keep up with it.
Time is just things changing, one after another. Without change, there is no time.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, for example: 'Mou, because my salt timer only showed time while the salt was running.' Then it is fair to Rekha: all clocks keep together, as if they all follow one time.
items.why: This is a real argument. Isaac Newton thought like Rekha. Aristotle and Nagarjuna thought more like Mou. Nobody has settled it.

items.p: In the banana card test, one person who reads Urdu laid the cards from right to left. What is the best reason?
opts: Urdu is written from right to left, and people often lay out time the way they read
He made a mistake
He did not understand the cards
items.why: Scientists have found that people often lay out time the way they read and write. Urdu and Arabic are written from right to left.

items.p: Draw the four banana cards the way one person in your family laid them out. Add an arrow to show which way time went.
items.a: Four cards in a row, from whole banana to peel, with an arrow from first to last.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the real order and the direction, and names the person.
items.art: Four empty card shapes in a row, with a space for an arrow underneath.

items.p: A clock can be steady and still show the wrong time.
items.why: True. A steady clock may have been set wrong. Being steady and being set right are two different things, and a good clock needs both.

items.p: Draw a line from each clock to the steady change it counts.
pairs: A shadow moving as the Earth turns
items.why: Every clock counts a steady change. The kinds of change are very different, but the idea is the same.

items.p: Which of these would make the worst clock?
opts: The Earth spinning
Salt running from a cone
How long it takes you to eat a plate of idli
A swinging weight on a string
items.why: Eating idli is fast on some days and slow on others. It is not steady, so it cannot keep time. The other three are steady changes.

items.p: In the clock hunt, the clocks at home did not all agree. Which clock would you trust, and how would you check it?
items.a: For example: 'The phone, because it sets itself from the network. I would check the others against it.'
items.why: A strong answer names a clock, gives a reason, and says how to check, for example by comparing several clocks.

items.p: Besides salt, what else at home could you use to time one minute? How would you check that it is steady?
items.a: For example: 'A bowl of water with a small hole, or counting 60 slow claps. I would time it three times and see if the answers are close.'
items.why: A strong answer picks a thing that changes steadily and checks it by repeating the test, as in the salt timer.

items.p: In the damp monsoon, the salt in a timer sticks and stops. What does this tell us about the timer that day?
opts: It is not steady that day, so it is a poor clock
It is a better clock than usual
It is still a perfect clock
items.why: A clock needs a steady change. Sticking salt runs unevenly, so the timer cannot be trusted until the salt is dry again.

items.p: Two different calendars can both be right about the same day.
items.why: True. Each calendar counts days in its own way, by the Sun or the Moon. The day itself is the same day.

applications: Trains and buses across India run on timetables, which only work because every station's clock shows the same Indian Standard Time.
Phones and maps find where you are by comparing signals from satellites, using very exact clocks on board.
Doctors and nurses time medicines, heartbeats and breaths.
Cooks time rice, eggs and sweets, with a clock or by counting pressure cooker whistles.
Farmers plan sowing and harvest by the calendar and the coming of the monsoon.

open_questions.q: Why does time only go forward?
open_questions.why_open: Many rules of physics work just as well backwards. Yet eggs break and never unbreak. Scientists have ideas about why, but no one is sure.

maths.problem: In the salt-timer test, one spoon of salt ran out in 20 seconds. How long will 3 spoons take?
maths.explain: The salt runs at a steady speed, so each spoon adds about 20 seconds. Count on: 20, 40, 60. 60 seconds is 1 minute.
maths.context: This is about the salt timer you made from a paper cone.
maths.why_maths: Counting on in equal steps lets us predict a long time from one short test.

maths.problem: Kavya, a girl in Class 2, makes a salt timer that takes 30 seconds. Her friend Arjun, a boy in Class 2, makes one that takes 20 seconds, with the same salt. Arjun says his timer is broken. Is he right?
maths.answer: No. Both timers can be steady. Arjun's cone probably has a bigger hole, so his salt runs out 10 seconds sooner.
maths.explain: 30 take away 20 is 10, so Arjun's is 10 seconds quicker. A timer is not broken if it is quick. It is good if it takes the same time every try.
maths.context: This is about two salt timers made from paper cones.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much quicker one timer is, and comparing tries shows whether each one is steady.

maths.problem: Divya, a girl in Class 2, has a birthday on the 20th of the month. Today is the 13th. How many loops does her paper chain need?
maths.explain: Count on from 13: 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20. That is 7 days, so 7 loops. It is exactly one week.
maths.context: This is about the paper-chain countdown, where you tear off one loop each morning.
maths.why_maths: Counting on along the calendar tells us how many days we must wait.

maths.problem: Pongal is 3 weeks away. Meena, a girl in Class 2, wants one loop for each day. How many loops does she need?
maths.explain: One week is 7 days. 3 weeks is 7 and 7 and 7. 7 and 7 make 14, and 14 and 7 make 21.
maths.context: This is about the paper-chain countdown to a festival.
maths.why_maths: Weeks are groups of 7 days, so adding 7s turns weeks into days.

roots.context: We have made a clock from salt, put events in order, and read calendars that count the same day in different ways. Now we ask what time tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Two spoons of salt took about twice as long to run out as one. The salt ran at a steady speed, so its amount showed how long had passed. Every clock works this way, by counting a steady change. Nobody has ever measured time without watching something change.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about time as if it were a thing flowing by on its own, and a clock as a box that holds it. But every clock we can find counts a change: salt running, a quartz crystal shaking, the Earth spinning.
deep_truth.evidence: In the salt-timer test, each spoonful took about the same time, and two spoonfuls took about twice as long. The cone showed time only while the salt was running. When it stopped, the timer showed nothing more.

three.who_am_i: You are changing all the time: growing, breathing, thinking. That is how you know that time is passing.
three.what_is_life: Living beings keep time too. You get hungry at lunchtime, crows fly home at dusk, and bean plants lift their leaves before the morning.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is always changing, and some of its changes are very steady: the Earth spins, the Moon goes round, the seasons return. People count these steady changes and call it time.

roots.thread: Time shows up only through change. Salt falls, the Earth turns, a child grows. The same steady change can be counted by a cone of salt, a clock, a calendar or a living body. Bean plants and crows sense the day's rhythm, remember that rhythm and get ready for what comes next, just as you feel sleepy at bedtime. Some scientists call these automatic body clocks. Every one of these clocks, of salt or of living cells, is a different way of keeping count of the same changing world.

teachings.source: Augustine of Hippo, Confessions, Book 11, chapter 14
teachings.teaching: Augustine, a thinker in North Africa about 1,600 years ago, wrote: 'What then is time? If nobody asks me, I know. If I try to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know.'
teachings.link: Everyone in your family uses time every day, but it is very hard to say what it is. Your salt timer gives one plain thing we can say: we know time by counting a steady change.

teachings.source: Nagarjuna, Mulamadhyamakakarika, chapter 19 (the examination of time)
teachings.teaching: Nagarjuna, a Buddhist teacher in India about 1,800 years ago, often linked with what is now Andhra Pradesh, taught that time does not exist on its own. It depends on things. If there were no things, there could be no time.
teachings.link: Your salt timer showed time only while the salt was running. When the salt stopped, it showed nothing more. Nagarjuna said something like this about all of time.

teachings.teaching: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, said that time is the counting of change, of what comes before and what comes after.
teachings.link: In the salt timer, you counted the salt that had run out, from before to after. That is just what Aristotle said time is.

science.text: The most exact clocks, atomic clocks, count very fast, very steady ticks inside caesium atoms. Since 1967, one second has been 9,192,631,770 of these ticks.
Whether time could pass in a world where nothing at all changed is still argued about by physicists and philosophers.

other_view.view: In 1687 Newton wrote that true time flows evenly by itself, whether anything changes or not. On his view, clocks do not make time by changing. They only try to keep up with a time that would go on even in an empty, still world. Many people today still picture time this way.

practice.title: Listen to time passing
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Listen to every sound you can hear. Notice when a sound starts and when it stops. Maybe a fan, a bird, a horn or a cooker. I will say 'stop' after a while. Then guess how long it was, and tell me how you knew time was passing.
practice.kid: Sit still. Close your eyes. Listen to each sound start and stop. When you open your eyes, guess how long it was.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that not everyone pictures time going the same way? This card tells the true story of women scientists and a community in Australia.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought everyone pictured time the same way, with the past on the left and the future on the right. In 1991, Barbara Tversky and her colleagues asked children and grown-ups who spoke English, Hebrew and Arabic to put events in order on a page. English speakers mostly went from left to right. Arabic speakers mostly went from right to left, the way they read. Then Lera Boroditsky and Alice Gaby went to Pormpuraaw, an Aboriginal community in Queensland, Australia. The people there speak Kuuk Thaayorre. In this language you do not say left or right. You say north, south, east and west, even for a cup on a table. The scientists gave people cards showing a banana being eaten, or a man growing older, and asked them to put the cards in order. People sat facing different directions on different days. Every time, they laid out time from east to west, wherever they were facing. The idea that everyone pictures time the same way was wrong.
how_we_found_out.who: Barbara Tversky and her colleagues, and Lera Boroditsky and Alice Gaby, working with Kuuk Thaayorre speakers in Pormpuraaw
how_we_found_out.when: 1991 (Tversky) and 2010 (Boroditsky and Gaby, published in the journal Psychological Science)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Everyone pictures time the same way, going from left to right.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman scientist sitting on the ground with an Aboriginal grandmother, who is laying picture cards of a banana being eaten in a row, with a compass arrow showing east to west.
